## From concept to reality in a year: 30 agents that act together expand ServiceTitan Max’s capability


When the Cloud reshaped the digital world more than a decade ago, ServiceTitan Co-Founder and CEO Ara Mahdessian’s task was to convince contractors it was their future, but the industry was behind the curve.


With AI, he said in Tuesday’s keynote address to open Pantheon 2026 in Orlando, ServiceTitan’s task is to make sure the home and commercial services industry leads the transformation.


To that end, at Pantheon 2025, the AI-powered, self-running contracting business was a concept. ServiceTitan launched Max with 50 contractors who would help build on that idea.


A year later, Max is no longer just a concept. Now, more than 30 AI agents draw on context across demand, field, and office to help customers better understand their business, determine what should happen next, and then execute and coordinate that work across connected workflows.


But rather than optimizing each workflow in isolation, Max can orchestrate nearly the entire business.


“The AI race is upon us,” Mahdessian told the thousands of contractors in attendance. “But … you are a different leader. AI is still emerging, but you are already leading from the front. … Last time, we had to convince you to catch up. This time, the trades are in a much better position.”


ServiceTitan’s Max customer base will approach 700 by the end of the year, Mahdessian said.


“The magnitude of this investment only makes sense if AI can completely revolutionize how we operate a business – a business that runs itself, and a business that gets better every day. That is what this is all about.”


### The trades example


To illustrate the importance of that point, Mahdessian broke down a residential service business into the tasks a contractor needs to get right, every day. They fall into three buckets: Generating demand, booking jobs, and selling the work.


Contractors know all those tasks matter. Doing all of them at once, and excellently all day every day, is another matter.


Human teams hit two limits: time and speed. A marketer can't retune ad spend every time capacity shifts.


A CSR can't take a call on one line and also answer a text within 15 seconds, before the customer turns to a competitor.


No manager can review every call and field recording to coach every employee every day.


"The only way to be great at everything, concurrently, all the time,” Mahdessian said, “is to automate it."


### What a year it has been


Building a brigade of AI agents alongside Max customers, Mahdessian told the crowd in Orlando, revealed two effects:


-


Small gains in leads, booking rates and average ticket compound into large revenue gains.


-


And the added revenue carries a higher margin, so profit grows faster than sales.


Mahdessian walked through a hypothetical contractor. With 10,000 leads, a 60% booking rate and an $800 average ticket, the business brings in $4.8 million. At a 10% margin, that means $480,000 in profit.


Improve each of those three metrics by 10%, and the same contractor generates 11,000 leads, books 66% of them and averages $880 a ticket. Revenue climbs to about $6.4 million.


“But the best part is, costs don’t have to increase proportionally,” Mahdessian said. “More leads from the same marketing budget, and more appointments from the leads coming in, and more revenue from the same truck rolls. A good chunk of the additional revenue from each truck goes straight to the bottom line.”


Revenue in that hypothetical only increased by 33%, he said, but profit doubled.


“That is how disproportionate this effect is on profit vs. revenue,” Mahdessian said. “If we can shrink the connection between revenue growth and cost growth, for the next two decades we don’t have to talk about profit margins


anymore. We can celebrate them instead.”


### How ServiceTitan Max helps us get there


That’s because the agents within Max will work together to get the best outcome, not just accomplish a single agent’s primary goal. There is shared context and shared judgment among the agents, Mahdessian said.


“What the voice agent hears, the dispatch agent will know,” he said. “Each agent works from the same formulas. We built a best-in-class lead scoring that predicts how much any appointment might be worth based on all the signals – what was said on the call, all the details about the home, the homeowner, the equipment and so-on. We built something similar for demand forecasting.”


There is also coordinated action and arbitration, built in.


“(And) one agent can ask another to act,” Mahdessian said. “A plan no longer stops at the agent boundaries. …


“When several agents can act, the system decides which one does, based on the highest estimated value for the lowest expected cost.”


What does that lead to?


“Outcomes improve assumptions, assumptions improve judgments, and judgments improve the next decision,” Mahdessian said. “It’s a system that gets better over time.”


All that, Mahdessian said, means the trades are better positioned for the AI shift than most industries.


“Whenever the technological disruption happens, the companies that leverage the innovation thrive, and the ones that don’t suffer a different fate,” Madessian said. “As we speak, every industry is chasing. But for once, this industry has the advantage.”


*-Mike Persinger*

## Late-night calls, two PE deals and a winning brand


Eric Van Dam's wife kept asking who was calling at 10 or 11 o'clock at night.


The caller was Tommy Mello, founder and CEO of A1 Garage Door Service. Mello wanted to learn everything he could before choosing a private equity firm to partner with for the first time and take his business to the next level. In 2019, A1 earned about $4 million in EBITDA, and Mello had questions. Van Dam, a managing director at Piper Sandler & Co., took the calls despite the late hour.


This week at Pantheon, the two shared a stage to talk about where those calls led: two private equity transactions, a company with more than $400 million in revenue and 1,400 employees, and a case for what comes after the first payout.


Build the company to be sold


Van Dam's first piece of advice, Mello said, was to hire a CFO. Audited financials, a quality of earnings report and a data cube followed. The finance team carries a sale, he said, and buyers spend about $5 million on diligence before they commit to a big deal.


"Don't bring a knife to a gunfight," Van Dam said. Private equity firms arrive with top law and accounting firms, so owners need advisors of their own. Mello said a competitive process gets the highest outcome.


### Vet the buyer like a spouse


Mello questioned firms as hard as they questioned him. He asked them about the last two or three deals and the multiple on invested capital. He asked for references, including companies where the investment went poorly. He asked what happens if the company misses the budget by 20% in a quarter. He, lightheartedly, compared the conversation to a prenuptial agreement.


“A good partner mostly asks questions,” Mello said. One of his was asking why receivables ran over 5%. A1's installers weren't collecting at every job. After retraining, Mello said, bottom-line margin climbed from 17% to 27%.


Van Dam said A1 reached $27 million in EBITDA over its first 15 years and added more than $75 million in the four years with a private equity partner.


### One playbook in every market


Mello said every A1 market runs the same pricebook, truck, uniform and software stack, with one call center and one dispatch center. Van Dam said buyers now look past shared systems to shared people and processes.


### "You gotta deal with people"


Mello talked about prioritizing the team at A1. He started something called the Dream Manager program. It’s part life coaching, part marriage counseling, Mello said. One six-month cohort of 60 employees lost 450 pounds, saved $400,000, paid off $500,000 in debt, welcomed three babies and bought 10 houses.


Plenty of investors are trying to figure out how to Uberize home services, Mello said. His answer is good luck, because "you gotta deal with people."


Two weeks ago, he said, a participant cried and told him he wished he could rejoin. The program, the man said, saved his life.


Mello said he doesn't have to be involved in the company anymore. He is anyway, because "it's so fun watching people win."
